context: core jumpform · vertical MEP spine & life-safety dominate

brief.intro: High-rise residential — ground plus ten storeys and above — is where vertical coordination stops being a secondary concern and becomes as important as the finishing programme itself. A slipformed or jumpformed concrete core leads the structure upward, typical floors follow a tight repeating cycle, and a full vertical MEP spine — wet and dry fire-fighting risers, domestic water risers, electrical risers, fire-alarm zoning, smoke control and lift shafts — must be built, tested and closed in step with that cycle. Finishing runs several floors behind structure in a continuous rolling wave rather than floor-by-floor stops, because with dozens of floors there is no time to wait: any trade that falls behind the wave is very expensive to recover. Life-safety commissioning — fire pumps, sprinkler flow tests, smoke-control interlocks with the lifts, fire-alarm cause-and-effect — is a genuine engineering exercise here, not a paperwork step, and it gates occupancy floor-band by floor-band.

glossary.plain: formwork systems that climb the core ahead of the typical floors, so the core is always several floors above the slab being cast.
a finishing sequence that runs continuously a fixed number of floors behind structure, rather than stopping floor by floor.
permanently water-filled vs empty fire-fighting pipes firefighters connect pumps or hoses to on each floor.
grouping detection and sounders by floor or compartment so an alarm can be located precisely.
pressurisation or extract systems, often linked to lift homing, that keep escape routes clear of smoke in a fire.
a heavy beam or slab that changes the column grid between a wider podium and the tower above.
a light building-management layer monitoring common-area plant, lifts and life-safety status, short of a full industrial BMS.
releasing completed groups of floors to the owner before the whole tower is finished.

must_get_right: Keep the core jumpform lead consistent — if it slows or speeds unevenly, every typical floor and every riser section behind it re-sequences.

Treat the vertical MEP spine (fire, water, electrical risers) as a structural-grade schedule driver, not an MEP afterthought — floor-by-floor testing must be built into the floor cycle, not squeezed after.
Run finishing as a genuine rolling wave a fixed number of floors behind structure — never let it try to catch up to the core.
Protect life-safety commissioning (fire pump, sprinkler flow, smoke control, fire-alarm cause-and-effect) with real float — it gates occupancy and re-tests are common.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Core and structure run a 6-day calendar, with a night shift on the core cycle where needed to protect the climb rate. MEP and finishing trades move to two shifts at peak to hold the rolling-wave offset behind structure. Life-safety commissioning runs on a focused daytime calendar to allow controlled access.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs core jumpform lead → typical-floor cycle → vertical MEP riser installation & floor-by-floor testing → rolling-wave finishing (held a fixed floor-offset behind) → life-safety commissioning (fire pump, sprinkler flow, smoke control, cause-and-effect) → phased floor-band handover. The core's climb rate is usually the true pacing driver for the whole tower; once it is fixed, every other front is scheduled as an offset behind it.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and a sample/mock-up floor are approved before rollout; riser and fire subcontractors are mobilised in step with the core climb rate; the structural engineer signs off the transfer structure before load-out above proceeds; a single mobilisation; phased handover aligned with fire-safety compartmentation by floor-band.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Multiple tower cranes and hoists are shared across structure, cladding and MEP delivery; the core climb-form crew works ahead and restricts access to the top floors; riser and finishing crews queue behind the structural front; life-safety commissioning needs controlled, low-occupancy access; noise/hours limits and public-safety exclusion zones apply around a tall site.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: core climb-rate slippage compounding through every trade behind it, riser testing failures found late after enclosure, and life-safety re-test loops (sprinkler flow, smoke-control interlocks). Contingency is held at the riser-to-finishing transition and before life-safety commissioning/handover, not spread across floors.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (floor-band summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 (floor-by-floor); expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead by unit/trade for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
